title: Gendered Impact of the Energy Crisis in Ukraine Assessment
text:
Against the backdrop of intensified attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, the country is preparing for its fifth winter since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. UN Women Ukraine has released the Gendered Impact of the Energy Crisis in Ukraine Assessment, describing how energy disruptions during the winter of 2025–2026 affected women and men and setting out recommendations to ensure their needs are taken into account in preparations for the coming winter.

The assessment also highlights the specific challenges faced by households with children, older people and persons with disabilities, as well as those who care for them. It underscores the need to pay greater attention to the specific needs and challenges faced by women, particularly their increased responsibilities for caring for family members.

This publication draws on a nationally representative survey of 1,200 adults across Ukraine, a dedicated survey of 800 adults in Kyiv, 10 key informant interviews and eight focus group discussions with women and men in Kyiv, Ivano-Frankivsk, Odesa and Kharkiv. It also sets out recommendations for gender-responsive preparations for the 2026–2027 winter, addressed to the Government of Ukraine at all levels, the United Nations Humanitarian Team, funding and humanitarian partners.

This assessment was commissioned by UN Women as part of its TransformCare Global Initiative and conducted by Voluntas, with funding from UK International Development from the UK government.

The views expressed in this publication are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily represent the views of UN Women, the United Nations or any of its affiliated organizations.

This publication was funded by UK International Development from the UK Government; however, the views expressed do not necessarily reflect the UK Government's official policies.

title: Ukraine: 64% surveyed feel unsafe in their communities, half do not plan to leave — Polish Humanitarian Action (PAH)
source: Polish Humanitarian Action - Polska Akcja Humanitarna
text:
Kyiv, 12 October 2026. A lack of money, affordable housing and support with relocation can leave people in danger even when they recognise the risks. These challenges were discussed at a Polish Humanitarian Action (PAH) press conference on protection needs in Ukraine.

PAH presented findings from its Protection Needs Assessment in 19 communities across Dnipropetrovska, Zaporizka, Mykolaivska, Sumska, Kharkivska and Khersonska oblasts. 63.8% of respondents considered their communities somewhat or completely unsafe. Meanwhile, 50.9% of all respondents did not plan to relocate within the following six months.

The press conference brought together María José Gómez González, PAH Country Director in Ukraine; Hanna Pomohalova, Head of Programs; and Nataliia Korniienko, Country Protection Manager. Hanna Pomohalova discussed how the findings inform PAH’s programmes and its work with local partners to reach people in war-affected communities. Nataliia Korniienko presented the assessment’s key findings on safety, financial pressures and access to services.

PAH emphasised that staying in a community under shelling does not always mean having a real choice. Leaving requires transport, money and somewhere to live. For older people and people with disabilities, health conditions, limited mobility and the need for someone to accompany them can create additional barriers.

“The people who most urgently need to leave a dangerous area may be precisely those who have the fewest possibilities of doing so. Leaving requires transport, money and somewhere to go. It can also mean abandoning your home, your work and the relationships that still give some continuity to a life profoundly disrupted by war,” said María José Gómez González. “Staying does not always mean choosing to stay. Sometimes it simply means having no other option.”

Financial hardship also affects people’s safety and health. 32.9% of respondents reported using at least one coping strategy that could worsen their circumstances. These included reducing spending on food, postponing medical treatment and utility payments, borrowing money or living in unsafe housing. 67.7% identified cash assistance as a priority need. These findings highlight the importance of financial support in preventing living conditions from deteriorating further.

The assessment also found that services can exist without being accessible to everyone.

Transport costs, physical barriers, difficulties with documents and digital services, and a lack of information can prevent people from receiving support. Older people, people with disabilities and residents of remote communities face particular difficulties.

As winter approaches, these barriers become especially important. María José Gómez González explained that a power outage can mean losing heating, water supplies or a working lift. For someone with limited mobility, this can make even a nearby shelter or assistance point inaccessible.

PAH highlighted the need to combine material assistance with practical support that helps people access it. Mobile teams, support when seeking services, accessible evacuation and cooperation with local organisations and authorities can help reach people who would otherwise miss out.

The assessment included 1,841 household surveys conducted in January 2026 and 53 key informant interviews conducted in December 2025. Its findings reflect conditions in the selected communities at the time of data collection and are not representative of the population of the six oblasts or Ukraine as a whole.

About Polish Humanitarian Action

Polish Humanitarian Action (PAH) is Poland’s largest and oldest humanitarian organisation, and has been working in Ukraine since 2014. Following the start of the full-scale war, PAH significantly expanded its operations, providing comprehensive humanitarian assistance to people affected by the war. The organisation works in the sectors of protection, cash assistance, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), shelter and non-food items, and supports the development of local partner organisations.

If you or your loved ones need humanitarian assistance or advice, you can contact the PAH hotline at 0 800 750 678 or email feedback.ukraine@pah.org.pl. The hotline operates Monday to Friday, from 10:00 to 17:00.

title: Ukraine: Dnipro: improving continuity of care for prisoners of war through coordination
source: International Committee of the Red Cross
text:
When a person deprived of liberty needs medical care, finding a doctor is only one step in a chain of response. Patients need to be examined in a timely manner, referred to a specialized health-care facility when necessary, receive the treatment they need, and be able to continue that treatment without interruption.

These were among the issues discussed at the recent Inter-Ministerial Coordination Working Meeting on “Medical Support for Prisoners of War,” held for the second time in Dnipro.

Representatives of the Ministry of Justice, Ministry of Health, Ministry of Defence, health-care facilities, and the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) came together for the meeting.

Support in detention

The ICRC has been working with health-care services for those deprived of liberty in Ukraine for many years, to improve conditions and provide support where needed.

Those deprived of liberty include soldiers in captivity as prisoners of war, who are generally held in places of internment, and detainees, who are those that have been judicially charged with a crime and are held in places of detention. There are times when each may be held in the same facility in separate areas. Regardless of the reason for being deprived of liberty, all have a right to medical treatment.

When coordination helps prevent interruptions in care

For internment or detention facilities in front-line regions, organizing medical care can be more challenging. People may need to be relocated or evacuated and, in some cases, referred to specialized health-care facilities. At the same time, treatment that has already begun needs to continue without interruption.

The first such meeting to discuss these challenges was held in Dnipro last year. Some of the solutions agreed on at that meeting have already resulted in practical changes.

One example was the opening of an X-ray department at Penal Institution No. 4, which began operating at the end of 2025. X-ray examinations can now be carried out on site, without transporting patients to another health-care facility.

The ICRC’s work towards consistent medical care involves not only dialogue and professional support, but also practical assistance. According to representatives of the State Criminal and Executive Service, the results of previous cooperation include support for an X-ray facility, the establishment of medical rooms, and the provision of other necessary equipment.

But equipment alone cannot overcome every challenge.

With more internment facilities now existing, more medical staff need to know where to refer a patient, who is responsible for the next stage of treatment, and how to transfer the necessary information. This is why inter-agency coordination remains an important part of the work.

“When health and prison authorities come together, they can better address the health-care needs of sick and wounded prisoners of war. Through this dialogue, the ICRC supports efforts to strengthen continuity of care and improve access to timely and appropriate health care, building on our long-standing work alongside detention health-care services in Ukraine,” says Stoycho Tihomirov Kitaev, deputy head of the ICRC Dnipro subdelegation.

The first such meeting to discuss these challenges was held in Dnipro last year. Some of the solutions agreed on at that meeting have already resulted in practical changes.

One example was the opening of an X-ray department at Penal Institution No. 4, which began operating at the end of 2025. X-ray examinations can now be carried out on site, without transporting patients to another health-care facility.

From capture to treatment

One of the key questions discussed at the recent meeting was very practical: what happens when a prisoner of war needs medical care that cannot be provided at the place of internment?

Participants discussed the patient pathway — where medical staff should turn when specialized treatment is needed, how a patient can receive care at Ministry of Health or Ministry of Justice facilities, and how to ensure continuity of any needed treatment until the prisoner of war is repatriated.

For Hanna Ostakhova, Head of the Dnipropetrovsk and Donetsk Regional Branch of the State Criminal and Executive Service Health Centre of the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine, working together as different institutions to find joint solutions is vital.

“It is important that, as a result of such meetings, we not only find practical solutions, but are also able to address them at the regulatory level,” she explains.

Throughout the year, we speak to each other frequently and resolve issues. But I would also like us to make progress on the legal side — so that the ways of resolving these issues are documented.”

title: Ukraine: Humanity & Inclusion’s (HI) statement on the use of Explosive Weapons in Populated Areas and the rising civilian toll (July – September 2026)
text:
Now in the fifth year of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, civilians continue to endure the catastrophic impact of explosive weapons in populated areas (EWIPA), facing destruction, displacement, and long-term humanitarian consequences. Between July and September 2026, Ukraine experienced some of the highest recorded civilian casualty levels since the beginning of the war with 8,330 casualties and a 90% rise compared to the same period last year1, driven by intensifying missile strikes, long-range drones, glide bombs, artillery shelling and short-range FPV drone attacks. During same period, Ukraine also ramped up its deep strike operations against targets inside Russian territory, which were accompanied by reported civilian casualties.

Recent months have been among the deadliest for civilians, bringing immense loss and suffering

Overall, the civilian toll in Ukraine since February 2022 to September 2026 has risen to 73,451 killed and injured, underscoring the devastating impact of indiscriminate assaults on civilians and the urgent need for strengthened humanitarian protection.

The actual extent of civilian harm – both casualties and infrastructure damage - is likely considerably higher as many reports of civilian harm, have not been possible to verify due to the lack of access to areas near frontline and to territories under Russian control.

Between July and September 2026, the UN documented an unrelenting civilian harm in Ukraine.

In July alone, 437 civilians were killed and 2,610 injured, making it the deadliest month since May 2022. Overall, during the first eight months of 2026, more civilians were killed and injured across Ukraine than in the entire year of 2025, underscoring the severe deterioration in civilian protection and the mounting human cost of the war.

Ukrainian airstrikes on Russian territory have also caused civilian casualties, from January to July 2026 at least 327 civilians were killed in Russia3. These figures originate solely from official Russian sources and have not been independently verified by international observers or monitoring missions and therefore must be treated with caution.

"Life in Kyiv is constant uncertainty: you don’t know if you will wake up alive in the morning or reach work safely when there are no shelters nearby and the power plant next to the metro station is under repeated attack. It is an evening reading Harry Potter with your child, suddenly interrupted by ballistic explosions outside the window and a rush to the corridor. It is watching a high-rise burn just a kilometer away, consoling yourself only with the thought that the playground beneath did not claim children’s lives. It is seeing the tears of fear in your child’s eyes every day. Life in Kyiv is no longer life — it is survival." — Inna, HI finance officer, Kyiv, September 2026.

Most destructive weapons for civilians

Russian forces’ use of explosive weapons continues to generate a consistent pattern of civilian harm. Ukrainian forces have also conducted strikes using drones and missiles, including on Russian territory, raising concerns about the protection of civilians.

Weapons Used by Russia

Long-Range Drones (Shahed-136/1314 ; Geran-3, Geran-4, Geran-55; Italmas and Gerbera strike drones)6

Russia has sharply escalated its use of jet-powered Geran drones against Ukraine, launching heavy-warhead systems deliberately targeting Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure and residential areas. Daily attacks in August and September saw hundreds deployed, with some assaults killing civilians in Kyiv and other cities.7

Between July and September 2026, Russian forces launched 16,086 long-range drones across Ukraine, marking one of the most intense periods of drone warfare in the conflict. The sheer scale of these attacks had horrific consequences for civilians, with widespread destruction of homes, infrastructure, and disruption of daily life. 89.

On 2 July, Russia launched 496 Shahed, Gerbera, and Italmas strike drones in a combined attack on Kyiv, one of the largest episodes of the month; the strikes killed at least 30 civilians, injured more than 97, and caused severe destruction to residential buildings, a hospital, a humanitarian warehouse, and critical city infrastructure10.

Short-Range Drones (FPV, Lancet-type, Hornet)

Russian forces continued to use FPV drones that target evacuation buses, humanitarian workers, and frontline towns. July saw the highest monthly civilian casualty toll from shortrange drones since the start of the full-scale war: 111 people killed and 710 injured, nearly one in four of the month's civilian casualties. These systems did not only strike people, but they can also hunt them: OHCHR has documented drone operators targeting civilians in cars and buses, people evacuating, and clearly marked ambulances, and in July an FPV drone destroyed a Red Cross emergency-response van moments after its crew arrived to treat casualties in Vilniansk, with deaths recorded among humanitarian workers and persons with disabilities, whose remain unable to safely relocate in time without proper support.

Aerial Bombs (Guided and Unguided)

Russia’s use of glide bombs remained at record levels, devastating residential areas in Kharkiv, Sumy and Donetsk. On July 2026 civilian casualties from aerial bombardments rose 143% compared to June, reaching 105 killed and 753 injured.11 Cruise and Ballistic Missiles (Iskander-M, S-400/KN-23, Zircon/Onyx antiship missiles; Kh-101, Kalibr).

Russia intensified missile attacks in July, with 429 missiles launched12. Civilian casualties from missiles and loitering munitions accounted for 38% of all harm (183 killed; 967 injured). The combined use of cruise and ballistic missiles, glide bombs, Shahed/Geran loitering munitions, and FPV drones by Russian forces has had a devastating impact on civilians. These weapons disproportionately affect the most vulnerable groups - children, persons with disabilities, women, and the elderly, causing extensive destruction of civilian infrastructure, including schools, hospitals, and medical facilities, and severely restricting access to essential services. The use of explosive weapons in populated areas is likely to result in international humanitarian law violations regarding fundamental principles of distinction, proportionality, and precautions.

Weapons Used by Ukraine

Long-Range Drones (UAVs and naval drones)

Between July and September 2026, Ukraine intensified its long-range strike drone campaign against Russian energy infrastructure, striking major refineries including Omsk, TANECO, Saratov, Ryazan, and Perm, and warehouse facilities, these operations caused shutdowns, fires, and widespread fuel shortages across Russia, reducing refining output to its lowest level in two decades1314 .

Cruise and Ballistic Missiles (Neptune, Flamingo cruise missile; FP-7 ballistic missile) Between July–September 2026, Ukrainian forces escalated long-range strikes on Russia using Neptune cruise missiles, Flamingo cruise missiles, and possibly FP-7 ballistic missiles. Targets included oil refineries (Gazpromneft Moscow, Novoshakhtinsk), UAV factories (Atlant-Aero), electronics plants (Karachev Elektrodetal), ports, and Russian Navy vessels. These attacks disrupted Russia’s energy infrastructure, forced refinery shutdowns, and weakened its Black Sea Fleet presence, with civilian casualties reported 1516.

title: SRSG Patten’s Video Remarks for the Launch of the State Targeted Social Programme of Ukraine for Combating Trafficking in Human Beings for the Period until 2030, 21 October 2026, Kyiv
source: UN Office of the SRSG on Sexual Violence in Conflict
text:
Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen,

I am grateful for the opportunity to deliver remarks on the occasion of the launch of the State Targeted Social Programme for Combating Trafficking in Human Beings until 2030. This event is much more than the acknowledgement of a crisis. It is a reaffirmation of your commitment to strengthening protection, justice and dignity for those most vulnerable to trafficking, exploitation and violence.

War creates a perfect storm for these heinous crimes to flourish as families are torn apart, societal structures crumble, and vulnerability escalates. The State Programme on Trafficking recognizes that trafficking risks have evolved in the context of armed conflict, displacement, family separation, economic hardship, and growing online threats and establishes a comprehensive normative framework which not only seeks to combat trafficking but also to support survivors in their long and arduous journey to recovery and justice. The State Programme is also groundbreaking in its recognition of the link between trafficking in persons and conflict-related sexual violence.

By acknowledging that survivors of conflict-related sexual violence face heightened vulnerabilities to trafficking and exploitation, Ukraine is embracing a forward-looking approach that reflects the realities of contemporary conflicts. This is fully aligned with the evolving international framework, including United Nations Security Council Resolutions 2331 and 2388, which emphasizes the importance of assistance and services for the physical, psychological and social recovery, rehabilitation and reintegration of survivors.

I commend the State Programme’s strong survivor-centered focus which is fully in line with Security Council resolution 2467 and places the dignity, rights, and recovery of survivors at the center of the response, while promoting improved victim identification, stronger referral mechanisms, and better access to legal, medical, psychological, and social services. We know from experience that meaningful recovery requires more than immediate protection. Survivors need sustained access to psychosocial support, rehabilitation services, legal assistance, and opportunities to rebuild their lives and reconnect with their communities. UN Action’s initiatives in Ukraine have demonstrated the value of integrated, survivor-centred approaches, including specialized rehabilitation programmes, strengthened referral pathways, and survivor-led networks that help individuals move from isolation toward recovery and empowerment. Particularly important has been the efforts to ensure that support is accessible to all survivors, including men and boys, whose experiences often remain hidden because of shame and stigma and obstacles to reporting.

I commend the State Programme for further advancing Ukraine’s implementation of key commitments under its European integration agenda, including the Rule of Law Road Map on Justice, Freedom and Security, while responding to recommendations of the Council of Europe and aligning with the EU acquis.

From the perspective of my Office, today’s launch is another tangible result of the cooperation established through the Framework of Cooperation on the Prevention and Response to Conflict-Related Sexual Violence, signed between the United Nations and the Government of Ukraine in 2022. One of the pillars of that Framework is trafficking for the purpose of sexual exploitation. In this regard, my office, through the Team of Experts on the Rule of Law and Sexual Violence in Conflict, has worked closely with the Inter-Agency Working Group and provided technical assistance and policy support to relevant Ukrainian authorities together with Ms. Zhukovska and La Strada, including through the joint deployment of technical expertise to Kyiv with United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime. Ultimately, the success of this new normative framework will be measured not by policies alone, but by its impact on people’s lives: by reducing vulnerability, expanding access to protection and justice, and helping survivors recover and rebuild their futures.

The United Nations remains fully committed to supporting Ukraine in the implementation of this ambitious Programme. We look forward to continuing our partnership with the Government, civil society, survivors, and international partners to ensure that trafficking in persons and conflict-related sexual violence is prevented, addressed, and ultimately eradicated.

Thank you.

title: Ukraine: Returns to unsafe frontline areas: exploring the drivers of return and the experiences of returnees in Khersonska Oblast, October 2026
text:
Introduction

While the scale of displacement in Ukraine has decreased compared with the first years of the full-scale invasion, returns continue to take place to areas within reach of the front line. Decisions to return often reflect an interplay of economic pressure during displacement, access to housing, family and care responsibilities, attachment to home, and access to familiar services. Understanding these factors and how they interact is important for humanitarian actors seeking to support people displacing from, returning to or remaining in areas where security risks persist.

In July 2026, REACH, in partnership with the NGO The Tenth of April, conducted a qualitative assessment to provide an understanding of why people return to unsafe areas of Khersonska Oblast, defined as within 0 to 30 kilometres of the front line, and the challenges they face upon returning. Data collection comprised 30 semi-structured interviews with returnees in Kherson city and in four rural settlements: Kyselivka, Posad-Pokrovske, Blahodatne and Klapaya. Interview data were analysed thematically. The assessment aims to inform targeting and response strategies for organisations engaged in return, reintegration and protection programming in the oblast and in other communities along the front line.

The assessment sought to answer three main research questions: What factors shaped respondents’ decisions to return to unsafe frontline areas of Khersonska Oblast, and how did their experiences during displacement influence these decisions? How did security considerations influence these decisions, alongside family, economic, housing and service considerations? And what did respondents face after return, including unmet needs, and under what conditions would they consider displacing again?

Key Findings

Return decisions had multiple drivers, with relational and emotional considerations mentioned most often. Emotional attachment to home (24/30) and family reasons, including reunification and care for relatives (19/30), were the drivers most frequently cited by respondents, followed by economic considerations (15/30) and property or land (14/30), such as returning to an owned home or continuing to work the land. Access to services and perceived security were mentioned less often. Most respondents described a combination of factors rather than a single reason for return.

Economic pressure during displacement shaped return decisions, particularly among respondents with more recent recorded displacement episodes. Respondents whose recorded displacement began in 2024–2026 more often cited rent, living costs and depleted savings as reasons they could not remain displaced (7/12, compared with 2/18 displaced in 2022). Respondents whose recorded displacement began in 20222 more often reported finding work or receiving internally displaced person (IDP) payments during displacement. For respondents who returned to their own homes, return removed rental costs but did not end financial pressure: several still faced unemployment, repair needs and utility costs after return.

Displacement and return patterns differed between respondents in Kherson city and in rural settlements. Compared with respondents in Kherson city, rural respondents had more often been displaced in 2022 (13/15, compared with 5/15) and within Ukraine (12/15, compared with 5/15), and all six respondents who described a planned return lived in rural settlements. Respondents in Kherson city had more often been displaced between 2024 and 2026 and abroad, sometimes for only a few months, and more often described the cost of displacement as a reason they could not remain displaced (7/15, compared with 2/15). Because settlement type, timing of displacement and place of displacement overlap closely, these differences cannot be attributed to any single characteristic.

Improved security was rarely cited as a reason for return. Six respondents (6/30) mentioned security, referring either to greater danger in their place of displacement or to specific local conditions at home, such as relative calm or the demining of fields. Four respondents said security did not influence their return decision. Several respondents reported that security had deteriorated since their return but had nevertheless remained. When discussing what would prompt them to leave again, respondents most often named a serious deterioration in security.

After return, respondents reported reconnecting with family and community, but more than half (16/30) also reported unmet needs, most often related to income and livelihoods, housing repairs, healthcare, utility costs and children’s education. Many of these needs appeared to continue from displacement, compounded by insecurity and damage in frontline areas and by savings depleted while away, rather than being created by return itself.

Return may be temporary, with intentions to stay often conditional on security and family circumstances. Of the 18 respondents who intended to remain in their settlement, 13 named a condition under which they would leave again. Across the sample, ten said they would leave if security worsened significantly and three only if their home were destroyed; others tied the decision to their children’s safety or to older relatives who would not leave. Where respondents considered where they would go, they mostly named nearby cities, such as Mykolaiv or Odesa, rather than a return abroad. Three respondents had already been displaced and returned more than once, indicating that for some, return is part of cyclical movement rather than a final decision.

Evacuation and relocation support that addresses both the journey to safety and the conditions needed to sustain displacement could make leaving more viable and reduce pressure to return to unsafe areas. Respondents’ accounts highlight the importance of keeping families together, supporting children and older relatives, and accessing suitable accommodation and care at the destination. Where feasible, safe relocation options close to home could also reflect respondents’ stated preferences. Experiences of brief or repeated displacement point to the value of flexible support that accommodates further movement and the possibility of return when conditions allow. Addressing these practical concerns could make evacuation a more viable option for households considering leaving should security conditions deteriorate again.

title: Crises collide in Ukraine as attacks intensify and support shrinks ahead of winter
text:
IRC data shows Ukrainians face increased financial hardship and gaps in health care in the deadliest year since the full-scale war began.

Attacks have widened far beyond the front line, driving displacement, loss and chronic distress, as over 90% of people surveyed fear missile and drone strikes.

Financial assistance and access to health services and medicines are the two biggest unmet needs in Ukraine as winter approaches, yet aid shrinks.

The IRC calls on donors to keep investing in Ukraine despite competing priorities.

Kyiv, Ukraine, October 15, 2026 — Ukraine is heading into winter following the deadliest months since the full-scale war began, as attacks on civilian infrastructure and populated areas widen and humanitarian assistance shrinks against growing needs. New data from the International Rescue Committee (IRC) shows how crises in Ukraine are compounding, with each unmet need and risk fueling the next.

Humanitarian assistance shrunk in every region monitored by the IRC, and some areas have received no aid for more than two years. Financial assistance and access to health services and medicines are the two most urgent needs. Yet financial distress is no longer only a question of purchasing power—it is pushing people to abandon their homes, deepening anxiety and eroding their ability to cope.

“As winter approaches, people in Ukraine face cold, illness, fear and lost income, and each makes the others worse,” said Alain Homsy, IRC country director in Ukraine. “People are increasingly exhausted and unable to cope with daily life under missile and drone strikes.”

The data shows that intensified attacks are the trigger of compounded crises, generating displacement, loss and chronic distress. Regardless of distance from the front line, most people surveyed fear missiles and drone strikes. In some regions, as many as 90% of people are in urgent need of financial aid, and up to 60% need health services and medicines. 70% of internally displaced families would like to return home but cannot because of the security situation.

With repeated rounds of talks failing to deliver a ceasefire, external support declining and the response shrinking, the war’s fatigue is deepening. The IRC calls on donors to maintain investment in Ukraine despite competing crises, and to ensure accountability for violations of international humanitarian and human rights law. Ukraine needs a complete pause in fighting to prevent further loss of life. Even then, the needs created by the war will outlast the conflict, and people will need support to begin rebuilding what has been lost.

The International Rescue Committee (IRC) in Ukraine has been operational since February 2022, delivering emergency aid, health care, and protection services to millions affected by the escalation of the war.

Note to editors:

This data draws on protection monitoring conducted by the International Rescue Committee (IRC) between January and June 2026, using a mixed-methods approach that combines 1,828 household surveys, 133 key informant interviews and direct observation, along with a review of secondary data. The analysis follows the Protection Analytical Framework, which structures each risk by threat, drivers, effects, most-affected groups and existing capacities. Monitoring took place in five oblasts where the IRC operates—Mykolaivska, Sumska, Kharkivska, Zaporizka and Dnipropetrovska—with fewer interviews conducted in Odeska, Khersonska and Donetska.
